<reason>PRO (Side B) built the cleaner path: a population-level mechanism story, then a consistent scale/dose-response attack on CON's best evidence (supervised trials are not consumer campaigns; strip the support and the effect goes). CON's strongest opening line—Chile and Mexico showed no turning point—was turned against it when PRO asked for any country where behaviour campaigns bent the curve; CON's A1 effectively abandoned its own standard and retreated to "supervised programs," which PRO's closing correctly identified as conceding the scale problem. On the compensation clash, PRO's asymmetry argument (removed sugar keeps working with no effort; coaching decays when it stops) plus the "snacking elsewhere concedes the shelf decides" turn was sharper than CON's "wash" claim. CON's whack-a-mole regress was its best late move but PRO reframed it as an argument for widening policy. CON also had a clipped opening and never squarely answered the app-abandonment/dose-response point. Both sides used plausible general knowledge without fake sourcing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2 A1/A2: accepting apps onto CON's ledger and then applying CON's own "bend the curve" test, combined with the directional asymmetry of compensation (effort-free benefit vs. decay by default), which forced CON to drop its own standard in [A4.1] and left "supervised" as the exposed weak point PRO's closing crystallized.</best_rebuttal>
